What does it take to make a shooter good in your opinion?
Nearly every gun should be useful if used correctly.

If we are talking multiplayer then my all time favorite was BF: Bad Company 2. It had:

  • optimal movement speed between twitch shooter and simulator

  • optimal balance between tight corridors and large open spaces

  • optimal map size in general

  • almost all guns/tools useful

  • no magical ability bullshit

  • fixed spawn points, no anti-camping auto spawn behind your back like COD

  • realistic "dirty looking" graphics without shiny effects

  • decent amount of destruction

The thing that makes or breaks most FPSes is the way motion is handled with the mouse... or... other... input devices. Games like Quake and Half-Life are so responsive compared to the CoD / Battlefield games, which feel floaty and disembodied. A game like Resident Evil has terrible shooting mechanics (it's in the horror category only because of how frightengly bad the controls are).

But after the physical connection is taken care of, it comes down to boredom. If enemies are just thrown at you in no particular pattern or given meaningless variation, it quickly becomes a slog. There should either be plot-related reasons enemies appear where they do and in what numbers OR there should be some new challenge introduced by their deployment configuration.

What really makes a shooter shine, though is clear move telegraphing as well as sound handling. For whatever reason sound reproduction is all over the place when it comes to games. Some games you can pinpoint anything with sound, others are completely crazy - like making your footsteps louder than you weapons, or sound like they are coming from right behind you as if you're being followed everywhere

Yeah you just touched on most of my pet peeves as well.

I fucking hate mouse smoothing with a passion, I'm convinced it's what is primarily responsible for the floaty disembodies feel you're talking about.

Sound is way too often overlooked as well, it can be just as if not more important than graphics IMO. I remember being incredibly impressed with Return to Castle Wolfenstein back in the day because it really nailed the positional sound.

I would like to see a realistic use of ammo. The average combat infantryman carries 10 mags of 5.56. (10 lbs) That is 33 seconds of fire power. Once he is out he is out. With 10 lbs. pf ammo, 8 lb rifle, 30 pounds of body armor, 10 (one pound) hand grenades we are looking at 60 lbs of weight. With that much weight you ain't going to be running and jumping all over the place. Most FPS shooters shoot up the 300 rounds in about a minute.

This is useful info, I'm not aiming to make a military shooter per-se but I am leaning heavily towards realism.

One of my favorite things about the original rainbow six games was they were the first I remember where magazines acted like magazines instead of some magical pool of bullets.

Does your average infantryman actually carry 10 grenades? that's more than I would have thought.

When I was in we carried 10 mags and four grenades. Typically 3 Frags and a smoke. We also carried as minimum 2 liters of water and an entrenching tool. When beyond the wire when you stop for only a few minutes you dig you a hasty cover. A slit trench gouged out of the earth a foot deep and as wide and long as your body will save you a world of hurt. The shrapnel and rock kicked up by an RPG travel out from the burst, (above ground level) If you are below ground level it flies over you or falls on you. When if falls on it is still hot but the velocity has been spent and now is under gravitational pull of the earth. (THE EARTH SUCKS) If close to you it still rings your chimes though.

Without going into the technical and game mechanics that make or break a game, the more general gameplay elements I look for when buying a shooter is for it to have a robust single player campaign. I'm not really a competitive multiplayer gamer because I'm too old to compete with teenagers and don't have enough time to practice often, though I still do play that way sometimes. I just really want a fun adventure story to jump into. I can forgive a lot of flaws if I'm into the adventure and the setting. I mostly tend to buy shooters that focus on the single player or co-op campaigns and have multiplayer elements as a secondary option.
